slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Policy and Legislative Analysis through an Equity Lens
Understand the policy question, examine proposed changes to law, and develop recommendations that make equity part of the work.
Advanced self-directed learning
slides.narration: A policy can shape the choices available to a person, the resources a service receives, and the responsibilities of staff and partners. This course develops your ability to examine those effects and make a well-supported recommendation. You will work with public Minnesota records on Waiver Reimagine and intervention and respite service redesign, consider different perspectives, and practice writing an analysis. Choose the opening conversation or read its transcript. Later, brief optional guidance is available where a concept deserves closer attention. Keep a decision relevant to your role in mind as you learn.
slides.title: Policy and Legislative Analysis through an Equity Lens
slides.body:
Understand the policy question, examine proposed changes to law, and develop recommendations that make equity part of the work.
Advanced self-directed learning

slides.text:
What are we analyzing?
A policy guides decisions and action.
Policy analysis examines a problem, compares responses, and assesses consequences.
Legislative analysis examines proposed changes to law.
Bill analysis identifies what specific provisions and amendments would change.
slides.narration: These activities overlap, but they ask different questions. A policy analyst may compare several ways to improve service access before any bill exists. Legislative analysis considers what changing the law would mean for services, resources, and responsibilities. Bill analysis then examines a particular text: what is added or removed, who must act, what conditions apply, and when a change would take effect. Equity belongs within each activity. The way a problem is defined affects which solutions receive serious consideration and whose experience counts as evidence. Think of an issue in your work: are you choosing an approach, examining proposed law, or interpreting a specific provision?
slides.title: What are we analyzing?
slides.body:
A policy guides decisions and action.
Policy analysis examines a problem, compares responses, and assesses consequences.
Legislative analysis examines proposed changes to law.
Bill analysis identifies what specific provisions and amendments would change.

slides.text:
What you will learn and practice
Read a provision and explain its practical meaning.
Weigh community experience alongside staff knowledge and other evidence.
Compare benefits, burdens, and resource needs.
Write a recommendation and revise it when the evidence or text changes.
slides.narration: Your final task is a short recommendation that a colleague could use in a real discussion. You will explain the question, compare options, and show why your preferred approach responds to the evidence. Start with your own contribution. Analysts bring close reading; program colleagues bring knowledge of services; fiscal colleagues bring cost questions; managers and leaders bring resource and implementation responsibilities. The consultant helps investigate equity concerns and develop alternatives. You do not need to hold every role. You do need to understand which questions your own expertise can answer and where another perspective would strengthen the analysis.

slides.text:
Waiver Reimagine provides a real case
The 2026 law adds advance budget and service information and a phased transition to the two-waiver structure.
DHS’s July 2026 update explains that a new launch date had not been determined.
Read the legal change and the dated implementation account together.
slides.narration: Waiver Reimagine concerns the structure of disability waivers and individual budgets. Minnesota Laws 2026, Chapter 121, Article 9, Section 51 adds requirements affecting planning and transition. The agency’s July 6 update explains what that means for implementation and states that launch could not occur by January 1, 2027. Those records answer different questions: the law describes requirements; the update describes the agency’s position at that date. Neither tells us how every person has experienced the change. We use these dated records to practice analysis, not to predict a launch date. A current operational assignment would also require checking for later official updates.

From legal language to people’s choices
Read the requirement
Understand the intended benefit
Examine people’s experience
Compare ways to carry it out
Recommend support and follow-through
slides.narration: Follow the relationship between the provision and its purpose. Advance information can give people time to consider support choices, but its usefulness depends on whether they can understand and discuss it. Your analysis could therefore examine explanations, opportunities to ask questions, and the preparation staff need. This diagram describes a way to reason through the course example. It is not a new agency approval sequence. At each point, ask what the evidence establishes and what remains a question. The recommendation should make the connection between the legal requirement, the person’s experience, and the proposed support easy to follow.

slides.text:
Practice reading the Waiver Reimagine change
The law adds advance planning information and phased implementation. The July 2026 DHS update says no new launch date has been set. Which conclusion is supported?
A. The requirement has changed; examine how people will receive and use the information during transition.
B. The new waiver arrangements are already operating for everyone because the Legislature acted.
C. The legal change is still only a suggestion because the launch date has not been set.
Choose a response to explore the reasoning.
slides.narration: Read the two records together before choosing. An enacted requirement establishes an obligation; an agency update can clarify the state of implementation. A useful briefing preserves both. Consider the practical effect of telling colleagues that a service has launched when the record does not say that, or treating a law as a draft because its implementation is still being prepared. Those errors could affect communications, planning, and the advice people receive. The strongest response identifies what is established and then asks a substantive question about how the requirement will support people’s choices.

slides.text:
A sound starting point for the analysis
This conclusion separates the requirement from implementation. It opens a useful equity question: can people use the information to make informed choices?
Examine communication, assistance, preparation time, and continuity of support.

What would you ask people who will use the planning information?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The first response reflects both records and identifies work the analysis can improve. You can now ask how different people would use the information, what staff need to explain, and what evidence would demonstrate understanding. Receiving information is not the same as being able to act on it. Consider whether the proposed explanation lets people ask questions about choices that matter to them. This is a contribution to a recommendation; it does not claim that a particular communication plan has been approved or tested.

slides.text:
Enactment does not establish everyone’s experience
A legal change does not prove that services have launched or that people have received usable support.
An inaccurate launch claim could mislead planning and communication. Use the dated implementation account and ask what people still need.

What would you ask people who will use the planning information?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The second response moves beyond the evidence. A colleague could repeat the claim in guidance or advise a person based on arrangements that are not yet available. The July update is explicit about launch uncertainty at that time. Keep that distinction in the analysis, then examine the choices still open in preparing people and staff. This does not weaken the recommendation. It makes the advice more dependable and directs attention to the practical work needed.

slides.text:
Implementation work does not undo the law
The launch date can remain unsettled while an enacted requirement is in place. Calling the provision a suggestion would overlook the direction it gives.
Separate what is required from the choices available in carrying it out.

What would you ask people who will use the planning information?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The third response confuses legal status with implementation timing. It could cause a team to leave required considerations out of its planning. A useful analysis identifies the obligation, checks the relevant effective language, and examines how to carry it out responsibly. Staff can compare ways to explain information or support participation while respecting the actual requirement. A recommendation should be clear about which part is a legal direction and which part is the team’s proposed approach.

slides.text:
Equity changes the substance of the analysis
Ask whose experience defines the problem, whose knowledge informs the evidence, and how each option distributes benefits and burdens.
Use the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit to deepen those questions throughout the work and explain how they affect the recommendation.
slides.narration: The public DHS Equity Policy includes legislative proposals, policy development, budgets, and service delivery within its equity-analysis expectations. The toolkit connects those responsibilities to the work. In this course, use it to examine the problem before settling on a solution, to identify perspectives that can test your assumptions, and to compare what each option would mean for different people. The result should be visible in the recommendation itself: an option changed, a burden addressed, or an unanswered question made explicit. The practice brief helps develop that judgment; it does not replace the agency’s required review.
slides.title: Equity changes the substance of the analysis
slides.body:

slides.text:
Trace the effect you expect to see
Start with a specific feature of the proposal. Explain what it asks people or staff to do and why that could change access, opportunity, or choice.
Consider disability, race, language, geography, and other conditions where they help explain the issue.
slides.narration: For the Waiver Reimagine example, a team might ask how someone understands a budget explanation well enough to discuss support choices. An accessible document may still leave an unanswered language question; a clear explanation may still arrive without enough opportunity for discussion. These are possibilities to investigate, not experiences to assign to a person because of identity. Look for evidence of the barrier and ask people about their actual experience. When the same requirement repeatedly disadvantages people facing a particular condition, consider whether the design needs to change rather than relying on exceptional help.
slides.title: Trace the effect you expect to see
slides.body:
Start with a specific feature of the proposal. Explain what it asks people or staff to do and why that could change access, opportunity, or choice.
Consider disability, race, language, geography, and other conditions where they help explain the issue.

slides.text:
Use culture briefs to ask better questions
A culture brief can prepare you to ask about trust, communication, participation, and experience with services.
It cannot predict an individual’s priorities. Check assumptions with people affected by the work and preserve differences within a community.
slides.narration: Suppose your initial engagement plan relies on a written invitation and a daytime meeting. A brief may prompt questions about language, accessibility, work schedules, trusted relationships, or how public discussion feels to participants. Ask which of those matters here rather than treating the brief as a profile of everyone invited. The same discipline applies to staff perspectives. No employee should be expected to represent an entire community because of identity. Record what people actually tell you and let it influence the options while choices remain open. You can prepare thoughtfully and still remain open to being surprised.

slides.body:

slides.text:
Whose knowledge influences the recommendation?
Bring legislative, program, fiscal, equity, and service experience into the discussion. Make room for staff who implement decisions as well as those who approve them.
Ask how contributions changed the recommendation, not only who attended.
slides.narration: A newer employee may notice an unclear instruction that experienced colleagues work around through informal contacts. A service partner may see a handoff problem that does not appear in an internal report. Managers can invite those observations early, share the material in advance, and make questions welcome across levels of seniority. Consider the employee life cycle: how new staff learn a change, how experienced staff receive updated guidance, and who has time and opportunity to contribute. If preparation depends on informal access, both service consistency and staff development can suffer. Leadership should be able to see the practical support the recommendation needs.

slides.text:
A second public example brings community evidence
DHS’s intervention and respite service redesign connects a legislatively directed study with service proposals and feedback.
Its 2026 survey summary raises concerns about overlapping services and provider responsibilities.
Use that concern to ask what a revised service design should clarify.
slides.narration: The 2023 law directed an evaluation of ways to expand access to specified services for people with disabilities and co-occurring behavioral health conditions. DHS’s later public material describes redesign work informed by partner input. The 2026 feedback includes confusion about how services fit together. For an analyst, that is a substantive issue: unclear responsibilities may affect whether people receive coordinated support. The next step in reasoning is to examine the relevant service language and identify what needs clarification. The course does not reconstruct private agency deliberations or claim that participants endorsed one particular remedy.

Respondents’ expectations about culturally specific needs

The largest group selected a positive response, while a substantial number were unsure or concerned. That pattern gives an analyst a reason to investigate what people understood by culturally specific needs and which aspects of the design they were considering. It does not establish that the design will work for every community. Notice the denominator: this item has 52 responses. Use that number for this comparison, rather than the total who provided feedback elsewhere in the survey.

slides.text:
Practice using community feedback
A draft recommendation cites the chart as evidence that the design meets every community’s needs. The survey report also identifies limited direct input from people using services. Which revision is strongest?
A. Keep the conclusion because the positive category contains more responses than either other category.
B. Describe the responses and limits, investigate concerns, and seek missing perspectives before settling the design.
C. Remove all community evidence because this survey cannot establish what every person needs.
Choose a response to explore the reasoning.
slides.narration: The positive responses matter, and so do uncertainty and participation limits. An analyst must decide what conclusion the evidence can reasonably support. Treating the result as universal agreement could close discussion before people most affected have shaped the design. Discarding the survey would also waste useful knowledge. Consider how to preserve the finding while identifying the additional experience needed. The recommendation should say how that input could affect the service design, rather than simply propose another meeting without a purpose.

links.text: A. Keep the conclusion because the positive category contains more responses than either other category.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Describe the responses and limits, investigate concerns, and seek missing perspectives before settling the design.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Remove all community evidence because this survey cannot establish what every person needs.

slides.text:
A larger category is not universal agreement
The result describes answers to one question. It does not represent every community or prove that needs will be met.
A universal conclusion could exclude concerns that should shape the design.

What could further community input change in the recommendation?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The first answer treats a comparison within the survey as a conclusion about everyone affected. The people who are unsure or concerned disappear from the reasoning, along with those who did not participate. A better account preserves the positive responses and asks what remains unresolved. The recommendation could identify a specific service feature to discuss with people using services, then explain how their experience would inform a revision. This is how participation becomes part of analysis rather than a count used to support a decision already made.

slides.text:
Use the evidence and address what it misses
This keeps useful feedback while making its limits clear. It turns missing perspectives into a specific question for the design.
Explain which choices remain open and how people will hear what changed.

What could further community input change in the recommendation?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The second answer gives the evidence an appropriate role. It supports a careful account of respondents’ expectations and a reason to investigate concerns more closely. It also respects people who have not yet had a meaningful opportunity to contribute. A useful invitation would identify the service questions still open, offer workable ways to participate, and explain how the feedback will be used. After a decision, report what changed and why some suggestions were not taken forward. Participation can strengthen a recommendation without implying that everyone must agree.

Incomplete evidence can still be useful
Discarding the survey would erase relevant concerns and ideas. Its limits call for careful interpretation and further inquiry.
Use what the responses support and identify the experience still needed.

What could further community input change in the recommendation?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The third answer sets an impossible condition: no single source can describe every individual. Community evidence can reveal an issue worth investigating even when it cannot estimate how common that issue is. Combine the survey with close reading, service knowledge, and direct engagement suited to the unanswered question. An account of confusing responsibilities, for example, can lead the team to examine whether the service description assigns those responsibilities clearly. The analysis becomes stronger through that comparison, not through rejecting all evidence that has limits.

slides.text:
Fiscal analysis and equity analysis inform each other
A fiscal note estimates the financial effects of a bill. It does not decide the bill’s merits.
Equity analysis also examines how benefits, costs, and effort are distributed. Ask who pays, who does the work, and whose burden an estimate may miss.
slides.narration: Minnesota’s Legislative Budget Office describes fiscal notes as official estimates prepared around the bill’s financial effects. They should not assume a change in law that the bill does not contain. When comparing policy options, work with fiscal colleagues to understand which resources are included and whose costs are being counted. Staff time, accessible communication, provider preparation, and unpaid family effort may raise different questions. A smaller estimated state expense is not, by itself, proof of a better outcome. Likewise, identifying an equity concern does not supply a cost estimate. Strong recommendations show how these contributions inform one another.
slides.title: Fiscal analysis and equity analysis inform each other
slides.body:
A fiscal note estimates the financial effects of a bill. It does not decide the bill’s merits.
Equity analysis also examines how benefits, costs, and effort are distributed. Ask who pays, who does the work, and whose burden an estimate may miss.

slides.text:
Make resource assumptions meaningful
For each option, ask what people must understand or do, who will support them, and what time and expertise that requires.
Separate a known cost from an estimate. Explain what could change the estimate and whether an apparent saving shifts work to someone else.
slides.narration: Return to advance planning information. A general publication, individual explanation, and supported discussion may require different resources and serve different needs. Fiscal and program colleagues can help examine staff preparation, assistance, translation or accessible formats, and coordination with partners. Community experience can reveal effort that internal budgets do not show. You are not being asked to invent prices. You are learning to ask a useful resource question: which assumption about people’s needs or staff work would most affect this option? That question can improve both the estimate and the proposed approach.
slides.title: Make resource assumptions meaningful
slides.body:
For each option, ask what people must understand or do, who will support them, and what time and expertise that requires.
Separate a known cost from an estimate. Explain what could change the estimate and whether an apparent saving shifts work to someone else.

slides.text:
Engagement should be able to change the answer
Identify the decision people can influence. Ask whose experience is missing and what may prevent participation.
Use their contribution to revise the comparison of options. Explain afterward what changed, what did not, and why.
slides.narration: A useful discussion about a service change might explore whether explanations support real choices, where people need assistance, and what creates uncertainty. That is more specific than asking whether people like the proposal. Culture briefs can inform preparation, while affected people define their own experience. Invite contributions in ways that fit that experience, and avoid assuming an established partner speaks for everyone. Within the workforce, create space for program, fiscal, service, and newer staff to question the draft. Meaningful inclusion concerns influence on the reasoning as well as an invitation to attend.
slides.title: Engagement should be able to change the answer
slides.body:
Identify the decision people can influence. Ask whose experience is missing and what may prevent participation.
Use their contribution to revise the comparison of options. Explain afterward what changed, what did not, and why.

slides.text:
Compare options against the same purpose
Use a clear purpose, such as helping people understand support choices during a transition.
Compare likely benefit, remaining barriers, staff and partner work, and evidence needed.
A recommendation should explain the tradeoff rather than hide it.
slides.narration: The next table presents approaches for consideration, not descriptions of an adopted DHS plan. Compare them against the same purpose. Broad guidance may reach many people but leave individual questions unanswered. Additional discussion could address those questions but needs time, expertise, and access. Involving people in reviewing explanations can improve relevance, yet participation must be planned and its influence made clear. You may combine useful elements rather than choose a single approach unchanged. Explain why the combination responds to the concern and what resources or evidence it still needs.

Compare ways to support informed choices
Approach | Potential benefit | Remaining question | Staff or partner work | Evidence needed
General guidance | Shared explanation | Individual questions? | Keep guidance clear | Can people use it?
Guidance and discussion | Tailored understanding | Who can participate? | Prepare staff to explain | Which questions persist?
Co-review and discussion | Improve relevance | Whose input is missing? | Hear and respond to input | What changed and helped?
slides.narration: These approaches are for discussion within the learning activity. None is presented as an approved communication plan. Consider which combination could help people understand choices while remaining practical for the staff and partners involved. Use the table to make the comparison explicit, then add a condition that matters in your role. A fiscal colleague might ask what delivery effort is assumed; program staff might ask how questions are answered consistently; the consultant might examine which perspectives are still absent. Your preferred option should address the concern you identified and explain why its additional work is worthwhile.

slides.text:
Changes in the text can change the advice
Compare the 2025 and 2026 Waiver Reimagine provisions. The later law replaces a fixed date in paragraph (g) with advance information tied to when a person’s services become subject to the budget, and adds phased implementation.
Revisit any conclusion that depends on the earlier wording.
slides.narration: In 2025, the provision set a July 1, 2026 deadline for the listed support-planning tool duties. The 2026 law removes that fixed date and adds information at least twelve months before services become subject to the budget. It also adds a phased approach and consultation with the Olmstead Implementation Office before seeking federal approval. These are real changes in enacted text. In an active legislative session, the same close comparison is needed when a bill is amended. Ask which recommendation, timing assumption, resource estimate, or communication now needs revision. Preserve evidence that still applies, but do not carry forward a conclusion that depends on superseded language.
slides.title: Changes in the text can change the advice
slides.body:
Compare the 2025 and 2026 Waiver Reimagine provisions. The later law replaces a fixed date in paragraph (g) with advance information tied to when a person’s services become subject to the budget, and adds phased implementation.
Revisit any conclusion that depends on the earlier wording.

slides.text:
Practice revising a conclusion after a change
Your practice brief was based on the 2025 fixed-date provision. You now have the 2026 amendment and the dated DHS explanation. What should you revise?
A. Keep the original timing conclusion because the purpose of informed choice has not changed.
B. Remove every remaining concern because the new transition language guarantees successful implementation.
C. Revise the timing and implications, retain relevant evidence, and ask what support people and staff still need.
Choose a response to explore the reasoning.
slides.narration: This activity asks you to use the change you just examined. The older concern about people understanding support choices may remain important, while advice based on the former deadline needs reconsideration. Keep the question about people’s experience and update the legal basis, timing, and practical implications. Do not assume that a new safeguard proves the intended benefit has occurred. A recommendation is more useful when a colleague can see what changed in the reasoning and why.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Keep the original timing conclusion because the purpose of informed choice has not changed.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Remove every remaining concern because the new transition language guarantees successful implementation.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Revise the timing and implications, retain relevant evidence, and ask what support people and staff still need.

slides.text:
The same purpose can require different advice
The purpose of informed choice remains relevant, but advice tied to the old deadline needs revision.
Show how the changed provision affects planning and communication while retaining useful evidence about people’s needs.

Which conclusion changes, and which equity question remains important?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The first response notices continuity in the purpose but misses a change that could affect decisions. A colleague might plan around an outdated deadline or misunderstand what must happen before a person is affected by the new budget. Retain the service and community evidence that remains relevant, then revisit the implications of the new wording. The habit to develop is purposeful comparison: which part of this recommendation depends on the text that changed?

slides.text:
A safeguard creates work as well as protection
Transition provisions can support informed choices without proving that everyone has usable information or assistance.
Examine how the intended protection will work for people facing different circumstances.

Which conclusion changes, and which equity question remains important?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The second response treats the presence of a safeguard as evidence that the desired experience already exists. The analysis still needs to consider how information will be understood and used, how staff will answer questions, and what practical barriers may remain. That is not a reason to disregard the improvement in the text. It is a reason to connect the improvement to the support needed to make it useful.

A stronger revision connects text and experience
This updates the legal basis and preserves relevant community and staff knowledge.
It lets the recommendation explain the changed timing, the intended benefit, and the practical support still needed.

slides.narration: The third response gives colleagues a current, reasoned basis for discussion. The comparison shows why some advice changes and why other questions remain. For example, preparation time may support choice only if people understand the information and can obtain answers. A fiscal or program colleague can then examine the resources needed for that support. The equity consideration is part of the revised recommendation rather than a sentence added after its main conclusions.

slides.text:
Write a recommendation someone can use
Explain the question and relevant provision. Compare the practical options, including benefits, burdens, and resources.
Recommend an approach and show how community and staff knowledge shaped it.
Name the question that could change your advice.
slides.narration: Write a short recommendation about helping people use advance planning information. Separate the verified legal basis from the approach you propose. Explain which barrier the approach addresses and why you prefer it over another reasonable option. Identify the contribution you need from a colleague or affected person before advice becomes more definite. Use the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit alongside this practice to examine the substance of the analysis. The goal is a useful contribution to the people responsible for the decision, not a claim that a practice response grants approval.
slides.title: Write a recommendation someone can use
slides.body:
Explain the question and relevant provision. Compare the practical options, including benefits, burdens, and resources.
Recommend an approach and show how community and staff knowledge shaped it.
Name the question that could change your advice.

writtenActivity.prompt: Write 120–180 words recommending how to support people’s understanding of advance planning information. Identify the relevant public record, compare two approaches, and explain the evidence and perspective still needed.
writtenActivity.feedback: A strong response links its recommendation to the purpose of informed choice, distinguishes the law from the proposed approach, explains a real tradeoff, and identifies how affected people and colleagues could change the advice. A weak response only promises to be equitable or repeats the provision without considering its practical effects.

slides.text:
From a recommendation to a useful change
Ask what staff, partners, and people receiving services need to make the approach work.
Consider preparation, clear responsibilities, usable communication, and follow-through.
Look for evidence of understanding and informed choice, not only a completed activity.
slides.narration: The course’s public examples show why recommendations must connect with practical conditions. A service explanation can be published without becoming useful to the person who needs it. A staff briefing can occur without resolving uncertainty about how to respond. Consider what evidence would help a team improve the approach: recurring questions, experience using explanations, or a pattern of people needing assistance that has not been planned. Leadership can use that information to support staff and reconsider resources. These are possible questions for follow-through, not findings that this course has established.

slides.text:
Rewrite the claim with a stronger argument
Claim to revise: “The new requirements ensure that everyone can make informed choices.”
Explain what the record establishes, what people need to use it, and how you would strengthen the recommendation.
Include a meaningful community or staff contribution.
slides.narration: One possible response is: “The updated requirements create an opportunity for advance planning. I recommend testing explanations with people using services and preparing staff to discuss individual questions. We should compare delivery options and resource needs before choosing the approach.” That response distinguishes the requirement from the proposed support. It could be strengthened further by naming a specific unanswered question, such as whether people can explain the choices available to them after receiving the information. Your wording may differ. What matters is that the analysis connects a provision, a practical concern, evidence, and a reasoned recommendation.

writtenActivity.prompt: Rewrite the displayed claim in three or four sentences. State one supported fact, one practical question, and one recommendation with a reason.
writtenActivity.feedback: Look for a clear distinction between a requirement and an observed result. The recommendation should respond to an identified need and show how participation or evidence would improve the choice.

slides.text:
Bring the learning into your responsibility
Analysts: which provision needs closer comparison?
Program and service staff: where could the approach fail in practice?
Fiscal colleagues: whose time or cost is missing?
Managers and leaders: whose knowledge and support are needed?
slides.narration: Choose the question closest to your responsibilities and apply it to a piece of work you can influence. If you supervise staff, consider whether people have preparation time and a real opportunity to contribute before a recommendation is settled. If you work with programs or partners, consider what you know about service experience that an analyst might otherwise miss. If you advise on resources, identify an assumption that needs examination. This approach can support ADSA goals involving disparities, engagement, staff development, and communication while also addressing a DSD need that does not fit a single goal label.

slides.text:
Make equity visible in the work product
A strong analysis explains the change, examines who is affected, compares reasonable options, and supports a recommendation.
Community knowledge, staff experience, and evidence should influence that reasoning.
Carry one improved question or recommendation into your work.
slides.narration: You have practiced distinguishing policy, legislative, and bill analysis; reading a real provision; interpreting community feedback; comparing options and resource questions; and revising advice when the text changes. The shared purpose is to improve the quality of the work and the experience of people affected by it. Return to your opening question: what would you want a colleague to explain before you could support a decision? Use that standard for your own analysis. The most useful recommendation lets others understand both its reason and the practical contribution they can make.

outcomes: Distinguish policy, legislative, bill, and fiscal analysis and explain their contributions to a recommendation.
Read an actual Minnesota provision and distinguish its requirements from implementation and observed results.
Use community knowledge, staff experience, and evidence to identify barriers and compare alternatives.
Explain resource needs and the distribution of benefits and burdens without treating an estimate as an outcome.
Write and revise a concise recommendation whose equity reasoning is visible in the work itself.
